records.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
records.summary: Saint Kitts and Nevis demands real caution. Part of the Eastern Caribbean decriminalisation wave (2022 court ruling); tiny population, tourist economy, no documented anti-trans violence pattern; no LGR.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges; Saint Kitts and Nevis decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 via such a challenge.

Nation News (Aug 2022): the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down anti-buggery laws - the ruling covering Saint Kitts and Nevis (Jamal Jeffers v Attorney General) decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct.

Outright International country overview for Saint Kitts and Nevis (updated March 2026): decriminalised in 2022 via Jamal Jeffers et al. v The Attorney General - Sections 56 and 57 of the Offences Against the Person Act contravened constitutional privacy and expression rights; no legal gender recognition; no non-discrimination laws.

Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance + ECADE UPR presentation (2025): decriminalisation in 2022 after civil-society court challenge; LGBTQ+ citizens included in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 but 'lack of tangible steps by the State'; discrimination in workplace, education, accommodation and hate speech still not illegal; LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement.

records.name: South Korea
records.summary:
South Korea is broadly workable — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. But the country has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (a gap not shared by EU peers), no same-sex marriage, and a conservative society where 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers.

Institutional friction is documented: the national human rights body flags a "transgender blind spot" in hospital wards (the Health Ministry can't answer how to accommodate trans patients); school bathrooms are a documented friction point for trans teens; and among trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military, 12% experienced sexual harassment or violence (this affects Korean conscripts, not foreign visitors). No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it). Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

sources.claim: Korea Times (July 2024): a court ruled that police advising an LGBTQ+ individual (undergoing gender correction) to avoid using public restrooms constituted an infringement of personal rights, awarding symbolic damages of 300,000 won - recognition that such remarks ignore the reality faced by LGBTQ people.
Yonhap (May 2024): a court ruled against mandating transgender surgery to change legal sex status - a significant ruling on the requirements for legal gender recognition in South Korea.

The Hankyoreh (March 2024): for trans teens in South Korea, even using school bathrooms involves safety questions - the youth support centre Dding Dong presented research on school practices that exclude trans students; first-person accounts of avoiding restrooms out of fear.

Korea Herald (Nov 2023): the NHRCK (national human rights commission) flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalization' - the Health Ministry rejected a request to devise hospitalisation guidelines for trans patients; separate men's/women's rooms leave trans and nonbinary patients in a blind spot; hospitals were merely 'recommended' to place trans patients in single rooms.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised in the military (Article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023) but legal for civilians; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (repeated proposals stalled); legal gender change requires medical intervention; the November 2022 Supreme Court ruling affirmed that having minor children is not grounds to refuse gender-marker change; intersex people largely unprotected.

Peer-reviewed study (Epidemiology and Health, June 2025): 'Being trans in Korea' - nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults documenting key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages.
HRW World Report 2025 South Korea chapter: overall positive human rights record amid political turmoil (martial law, impeachment); includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section.

misterb&b gay travel guide to South Korea safety (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods but requiring contextual understanding - military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry covers the South Korean Supreme Court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

HRW (Aug 2017): 'South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights' - the National Health Insurance Service was ordered to pay benefits to a same-sex partner, affirming equal treatment; a significant judicial step amid the military's ongoing anti-gay witch-hunts.

records.name: Kuwait
records.summary:
Kuwait is dangerous for trans visitors — the least hostile of the Gulf states, but not safe. In 2007, Article 198 of the Penal Code criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" (up to 1 year in jail); within two weeks at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops, and taxis, three were beaten (one into unconsciousness), and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under this law.

However, in February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down Article 198 as unconstitutional — the only Gulf state to repeal its cross-dressing statute. The repeal has teeth: a cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut won 4,000 KWD in compensation, with the Court of Cassation ruling police had arrested her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait.

But the repeal is incomplete in practice: HRW reports transgender people "continue to face threats and harassment," and in December 2022 security forces carried out mass deportations of LGBT people under "security" measures. For a trans traveler: no criminal exposure for gender expression itself, courts now provide recourse, but police harassment and deportation risk remain real.

sources.claim: Brian Whitaker's overview essay (2016) on transgender issues in the Middle East: gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable; notes 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in Kuwait among other countries; discusses cross-dressing as a crime across the region.

Human Rights Watch (Jan 2008): 'Kuwait: Repressive Dress-Code Law Encourages Police Abuse' — Penal Code Article 198 criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' invites arbitrary arrest and abuse of gender-nonconforming people.
Human Rights Watch (Feb 2022): 'Kuwait Court Rules Anti-Transgender Law Unconstitutional' — the Constitutional Court strikes down the Article 198 'imitating the opposite sex' ban.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry covers the same Kuwait Constitutional Court ruling striking down Article 198.

US State Department 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Kuwait - significant issues include laws criminalising consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults 'which were enforced', torture reports, arbitrary detention, restrictions on expression and assembly, and extensive gender-based violence.

HRW World Report 2024 Kuwait chapter: authorities used penal code, national security and cybercrime laws to restrict speech; includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section; notes gender-segregation decisions at Kuwait University.

Cairo 52 (July 2024): analysis of steps forward after the abolition of Article 198 - the 2007 amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex in any way' (proposed by Islamist MP Al-Tabtabaei) was struck down by the Constitutional Court in 2022; the article traces the law's origins and impact on gender-nonconforming people.
DAWN MENA: transgender discrimination continues in Kuwait despite the court ruling - enforcement and social discrimination persist after Article 198 was struck down.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Kuwait's criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.

records.name: Laos
records.summary: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, and Laos has a socially visible tradition of trans feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation (the one-party state restricts all civil society), and no documented recourse. Vientiane and Luang Prabang are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque state) more than violent.

sources.claim: UNAIDS Laws and Policies analytics page for the Lao PDR filtered to transgender-related laws and policies - a database interface showing legal instruments affecting trans people in Laos (no criminalisation of same-sex conduct; limited specific protections).
ADB publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in Asia and the Pacific - regional comparative overview covering Laos among other countries.

Human Dignity Trust: 'A History of LGBT Criminalisation' - almost 500 years of outlawing LGBT people; overview of jurisdictions that criminalise and strategic litigation worldwide (Laos context: no current criminalisation but no protections).

GlobalGayz 'Gay Laos: Lost and Found' (2000/2009): Richard Ammon's account of a small Vientiane lesbigay circle - restaurants, friendships, romantic relationships; a picture of quiet, low-key gay life in communist Laos.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2018): 'Overcoming a government crackdown on social media in Laos' - 'net idols' face retribution for online posts; 'You can't post anything about the government' - the free-expression climate that constrains LGBT visibility.

EU External Action Service: the EU celebrated IDAHO day (International Day Against Homophobia) in Vientiane - diplomatic visibility for LGBT rights in Laos (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

records.name: Lebanon
records.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Lebanon: de facto and explicit criminalisation of trans expression (especially trans women) under Penal Code provisions; rising prejudice and violence in Beirut including attacks by state-affiliated militia groups on queer spaces after a decriminalisation bill was introduced; gradual progress on legal gender recognition since a 2015 judge's ruling emphasising the significance of transitioning; gender-affirming healthcare not prohibited and comparatively accessible, though privatised healthcare limits options.
EUAA Lebanon Country Focus, section 7.5 'LGBTIQ persons, including activists': assessment of the situation of LGBTIQ persons in Lebanon.
Human Rights Watch (Apr 2022): 'Tough Territory for Transgender People in the Middle East and North Africa' — regional survey incl. Lebanon on LGR requirements and enforcement.

Manara Magazine essay by Nora Noralla (March 2022): 'Confused Judiciary & Transgender Rights' - inside MENA case law on legal gender recognition in Lebanon, Egypt, Kuwait and the UAE; no legislative framework forces trans people into lengthy, costly judicial review where judges rely on outdated medical practices, selective Sharia readings and socio-religious bias, producing inconsistent rulings.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 534 ('sexual intercourse contrary to the order of nature') is regularly used for arrests; several courts have ruled it does not apply to same-sex relations but it remains in force; trans people can change markers only after surgical procedures; in June 2022 the Interior Ministry banned gatherings 'promoting sexual perversion'; the 'soldiers of God' group attacked queer bars and drag shows; Helem denounced the 2024 murder of a trans woman.
HRW (May 2018): 'Lebanon: Police Shutter Pride Events' - security forces forced cancellation of Beirut Pride events and detained organisers, using 'debauchery' charges and pressure on venues.

The Daily Beast (May 2018): profile of Georges Azzi - co-founder of Helem (the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, 2004), repeatedly dragged to Beirut police stations for interrogation and psychological pressure; now executive director of the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning across MENA; received OutRight's Felipa De Souza Award.

HRW (Feb 2017): 'Lebanon Edges Closer to Decriminalizing Same-Sex Conduct' - a judge ruled that consensual same-sex conduct is not 'against nature', building on earlier rulings interpreting Article 534 narrowly.

records.name: Liberia
records.summary: Liberia is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (Oct 2024): Liberian Representative Johnson Williams seeks supporters for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill - raising penalties to 10 years (life for repeat/'aggravated' offences), imprisoning children as young as 10, and outlawing LGBTIQ+ advocacy and 'promotion of homosexuality'; so far he has announced no success attracting supporters.

UNDP/OHCHR 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia Country Report' (April 2020): participatory review and analysis of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.

NPR (April 2012): 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight' - anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation calls for longer jail terms for homosexuality; fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (March 2012): Nobel peace prize winner President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended Liberia's law criminalising homosexual acts - 'We like ourselves just the way we are' - in a joint interview with a visibly uncomfortable Tony Blair.

records.name: Libya
records.summary:
Libya is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises “illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” (up to 5 years), and Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term “gender” haram, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no LGR, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Libya: de facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition (social, medical, surgical) via 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings designate the term 'gender' as haram, exposing users to punishment; no legal gender recognition framework or court attempts; armed militias retaliate against gender-diverse people amid the post-2011 conflict.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity criminalised (up to 5 years under 'illicit sexual intercourse' and 'indecent acts' provisions applying to men and women); no SOGISC protections; no legal gender recognition; enforcement and repression intensified after 2011 - armed groups and security agencies arrest people based on perceived orientation or gender identity, with discrimination, violence and arbitrary detention.

The Guardian (June 2016): Brian Whitaker's 'Everything you need to know about being gay in Muslim countries' - the official fiction is that gay people don't exist in the Middle East; family and societal attitudes are often a bigger problem than state persecution; Libya among the countries covered.
HRW (June 2015): 'Islamic State's War on Gays' - documents ISIS executions of men accused of homosexuality in territories it controlled, including in Libya.

D+C (June 2015): 'The situation for homosexuals in Libya is getting worse' - ISIS executed three young men in Derna (kneeling in plastic tubs, shot in the back of the head before a crowd); considered the first death sentence against homosexuals in modern Libya's history; no one in Derna dares speak of the killings.

HuffPost (Nov 2012): report that 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and death by a Libyan militia - NOTE: the original source was a Facebook page falsely claiming HRW affiliation, which later apologised for misrepresenting itself; treat with caution.

records.name: Saint Lucia
records.summary: Saint Lucia demands real caution. The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down sodomy/gross-indecency laws in July 2025 (Randall Theodule v AG) — the region's most recent decriminalisation, welcomed by the IACHR. Saint Lucia has a relatively organised community (ECADE, United and Strong) and hosts Pride. No LGR.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2025): 'Saint Lucia High Court Decriminalizes Same-Sex Conduct' — the court rules the 'gross indecency' and 'unnatural offences' provisions violate constitutional protections.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust case digest covers Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia - the constitutional challenge that decriminalised same-sex conduct.

Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2017): Caribbean activists (United and Strong of St Lucia, ECADE) protested PinkNews's framing of a Stonewall charity auction of a St Lucia holiday - 'Nothing about us without us'; St Lucia's law carries up to 10 years for gay sex.
AP News: St Lucia court ruling that criminalising gay sex is unconstitutional - the Eastern Caribbean litigation striking down the colonial-era law (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

United and Strong St Lucia (May 2015): human-rights sensitisation training for law enforcement - extending 2014 RSLPF training to Air/Sea Ports, Customs and Corrections officers, facilitated by Maurice Tomlinson; part of advocacy to reduce discrimination and achieve equality.
